intent: Test wheel_track 0.14 m (from 0.12) as a single-variable change on the iteration 9 platform (±0.03 m outer sensors at y = 0.04, 15 mm spacing, 0.016 footprint, 0.18 m / 0.8 kg body, 0.03 m wheel radius). Expected: slalom line_loss_events falls below 1 and slalom progress rises above 0.10, with oval completions held at or near 8 of 20 and a score at or above about 271. If oval completions fall and the score drops well below 271, the lower steering gain from the wider track is the cause, and the next step is to return to 0.12 m or test 0.10 m.
learning: Iteration 9 (271.06) showed that under the new damping, the ±0.03 m layout gives 8 oval completions and s-bend progress 0.44, so the reach and footprint are sufficient. Iteration 8 repeated iteration 7 exactly, so the simulator is deterministic for a fixed design and single-variable tests are reliable. The Integrator's feedback mislabels iteration 7 as ±0.036; the outcome table is correct. Slalom line loss of about 1 persists in every race and is the remaining gap, so this iteration tests the one untested geometry lever, wheel_track. Ask the Integrator whether the controller's kp or kd needs retuning to match the new steering gain if the robot becomes sluggish, and whether the slalom line loss clears.
rationale: Iteration 9 is the best raced result at 271.06, up from 160.5 at iterations 7 and 8. The geometry was unchanged across 7, 8 and 9, so the 110-point gain came from the controller. The oval now finishes 8 of 20 trials (mean progress 0.91) and the s-bend progress rose to 0.44, which means the ±0.03 m reach with 15 mm spacing, y = 0.04, 0.016 footprint and the 0.18 m / 0.8 kg body is confirmed under the new damping. The Integrator's feedback sets the rule for this case: if the score holds near the best result with oval completions kept, keep ±0.03 m and y = 0.04, and test wheel_track as a single-variable change. Slalom line_loss_events is still 1.0 at iteration 9 with slalom progress near 0.10, so the Integrator's condition for testing wheel_track is met. Iterations 2 and 3 showed body changes cost progress, so body_length, mass and body_width stay fixed. Changing wheel_track from 0.12 to 0.14 m reduces yaw per unit wheel differential by about 14 percent, which changes the effective steering gain. This is a single-variable test. I expect slalom line loss to fall toward 0 if the line is being lost in tight bends because the robot turns too fast, and I expect s-bend and oval progress to hold. The main risk is a slower response on bends, which would show as lower oval completions. I will read the result against iteration 9's 271.06.
